---
title: "Gibbard's Oligarchy Theorem"
format: typst
---

CCSW Ch A1\* pp. 289–293, with Ch 4 for the prose version. This picks up exactly
where the Arrow handout left off. We established there that the only place the
Arrow proof uses anything stronger than transitivity of strict preference is one
subcase of Contraction. The obvious next question is what you get if you refuse
that step, and the answer is Gibbard's.

A piece of history worth having: this was originally a term paper for a class
taught jointly by Arrow, Rawls and Sen at Harvard in the spring of 1969. Allan
Gibbard was then a graduate student, and later spent most of his career in the
Michigan philosophy department.

# The weakened framework

A **social decision function** (SDF) drops the demand that $R$ be an ordering.
It requires only that $R$ be reflexive and complete, and that it generate a
choice function: $C(S, R)$ is non-empty for every non-empty $S$.

By Lemma 1\*k, quasi-transitivity is enough for that over a finite set. So
consider SDFs yielding **quasi-transitive** $R$:
$$xPy \ \&\ yPz \to xPz \qquad (PP)$$
and nothing more. Indifference may be intransitive, and the mixed cases $PI$ and
$IP$ may fail.

Keep U, $I^2$ and P. Keep $H$ finite and $\#X \geq 3$.

Two notions beyond decisiveness:

- $G$ is **semi-decisive** over the ordered pair $(x,y)$ iff $xP_iy$ for every
  $i \in G$ implies $xRy$, whatever anyone outside $G$ prefers.
- $G$ (or a person) **has a veto** iff it is semi-decisive over every ordered
  pair. Nobody can be ranked above your choice over your objection. You cannot
  force an outcome, but you can stop one.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**T.A1\*.4 (Gibbard 1969).** If $H$ is finite and $\#X \geq 3$, then any SDF
satisfying U, $I^2$ and P, and yielding quasi-transitive social preference, is
**oligarchic**: there is a unique group $G^*$ that is decisive, and every member
of $G^*$ has a veto.
:::

# Step 1: what survives

**Spread of Decisiveness (T.A1\*.2) still holds.** Every transitivity appeal in
that proof chained strict preferences only, so $PP$ is all it ever used. Local
decisiveness over one pair still gives global decisiveness.

**Veto-Spread.** If $G$ is semi-decisive over one ordered pair, it is
semi-decisive over every one, and so has a veto.

*Proof.* Let $G$ be semi-decisive over $(x,y)$ and take any $(a,b)$, with all
four distinct for now. Consider:

| | Constraints imposed |
|:---|:---|
| Everyone in $G$ | $a \succ x \succ y \succ b$ |
| Everyone outside $G$ | $a \succ x$, and $y \succ b$ |

By P, $aPx$ and $yPb$. By semi-decisiveness, $xRy$, which is to say
$\sim(yPx)$.

Suppose $bPa$. Then $yPb$ and $bPa$ give $yPa$ by $PP$, and $yPa$ with $aPx$
gives $yPx$ by $PP$ again. That contradicts $xRy$. So $aRb$.

Nobody outside $G$ was given a ranking of $a$ against $b$, so by $I^2$ this
holds however those rankings are filled in. $G$ is semi-decisive over $(a,b)$.
The overlap cases run as they did for Spread. $\blacksquare$

Notice that this proof is the Spread proof with the conclusion weakened from
$aPb$ to $aRb$ and the input weakened to match. Vetoes spread for exactly the
reason decisiveness does.

# Step 2: decisive sets are closed under intersection

This is the step that replaces Contraction, and it is where the real difference
lies.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Lemma.** If $G_1$ and $G_2$ are both decisive, then $G_1 \cap G_2$ is decisive
(and in particular non-empty).
:::

*Proof.* Take distinct $x, y, z$ and consider:

| | Constraints imposed |
|:---|:---|
| $G_1 \cap G_2$ | $x \succ y \succ z$ |
| $G_1 \setminus G_2$ | $x \succ y$, with $z$ unplaced |
| $G_2 \setminus G_1$ | $y \succ z$, with $x$ unplaced |
| Everyone else | nothing |

Everyone in $G_1$ prefers $x$ to $y$, so $xPy$. Everyone in $G_2$ prefers $y$ to
$z$, so $yPz$. By $PP$, $xPz$.

Who has been given a ranking of $x$ against $z$? Only $G_1 \cap G_2$, who all
prefer $x$. Those in $G_1 \setminus G_2$ have $z$ unplaced, those in
$G_2 \setminus G_1$ have $x$ unplaced, and the rest were given nothing. So by
$I^2$, $G_1 \cap G_2$ is locally decisive over $(x,z)$, and by Spread it is
decisive.

For non-emptiness: if $G_1 \cap G_2$ were empty, fill in the free rankings so
that everyone prefers $z$ to $x$. Pareto gives $zPx$, contradicting the $xPz$
we just derived. $\blacksquare$

This is clause (4) of the filter conditions at the end of the chapter. Under
full transitivity the decisive sets form an *ultra*-filter, and an ultra-filter
on a finite set collapses to a single person. Under quasi-transitivity they form
only a filter, which collapses to a non-empty group instead.

# Step 3: the oligarchy

$H$ is decisive by P, and $H$ is finite, so there are finitely many decisive
sets. By Step 2 their intersection
$$G^* = \bigcap \{G : G \text{ is decisive}\}$$
is decisive and non-empty. It is contained in every decisive set, so it is the
unique minimal one.

**Every member of $G^*$ has a veto.** If $G^* = \{i\}$ then $i$ is a dictator
and has a veto outright. So suppose $|G^*| \geq 2$ and take $i \in G^*$. Put
$G^1 = \{i\}$ and $G^2 = G^* \setminus \{i\}$, both non-empty, and run the
Contraction profile:

| | Constraints imposed | Left open |
|:---|:---|:---|
| $i$ | $x \succ y$, $x \succ z$ | $y$ against $z$ |
| Everyone in $G^* \setminus \{i\}$ | $x \succ y$, $z \succ y$ | $x$ against $z$ |
| Everyone else | nothing | everything |

Everyone in $G^*$ prefers $x$ to $y$, and $G^*$ is decisive, so $xPy$.

Suppose $zPx$. Then $PP$ gives $zPy$. Only $G^*\setminus\{i\}$ were given a
ranking of $z$ against $y$, so by $I^2$ and Spread, $G^*\setminus\{i\}$ is
decisive. That is a proper subset of the minimal decisive set, which is
impossible.

So $\sim(zPx)$, and by completeness $xRz$. Only $i$ was given a ranking of $x$
against $z$. By $I^2$, $i$ is semi-decisive over $(x,z)$, and by Veto-Spread,
$i$ has a veto. $\blacksquare$

# Where the Arrow proof broke

Side by side, the single step that differs:

| | Full transitivity | Quasi-transitivity |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Case $zPx$ | $zPy$ by $PP$; $G^2$ decisive | same |
| Case $zIx$ | $zPy$ by $IP$; $G^2$ decisive | $IP$ unavailable |
| Case $xPz$ | $G^1$ decisive | only $xRz$, so $G^1$ is semi-decisive |

Under transitivity, both branches deliver a *decisive* proper subset, so the
contraction runs all the way down to one person. Under quasi-transitivity, one
branch delivers only a *semi*-decisive subset, which gives a veto rather than
decisiveness, and the contraction halts.

Dictatorship was never removed. It was divided.

# The example to keep in mind

The **Pareto-extension rule**: $xPy$ iff everyone prefers $x$ to $y$, and $xIy$
otherwise.

- Reflexive, complete, quasi-transitive, and satisfies U, $I^2$, P and D.
- $IP$ fails: let person 1 rank $x \succ y \succ z$ and person 2 rank
  $y \succ z \succ x$. Then $yPz$ and $xIy$, but $xIz$ rather than $xPz$.
- The only decisive set is $H$ itself, so $G^* = H$ and every person has a veto.

This is the case we met in Class 16 as the third way of completing the Pareto
quasi-ordering. Sen's verdict there was that it is "a rather arbitrary rule".
Gibbard's theorem says something sharper: it is the *most democratic* member of
the permissible class, because it spreads the veto as widely as it can go. Every
other quasi-transitive rule concentrates the veto in a smaller group.

Sen's own assessment:

> While the existence of vetoers may be less unattractive than that of a
> dictator, it is unappetizing enough in failing to provide what can reasonably
> be seen as a grand resolution of the Arrow problem.

# Where this leaves the escape route

Weakening further does not help. Acyclicity is weaker than quasi-transitivity,
and Mas-Colell and Sonnenschein (1972) showed it still yields a vetoer;
Blair and Deb's NIM result (T.A1\*.5) gets a vetoer from acyclicity plus
neutrality and monotonicity. Blair and Pollak (1982) showed that even dropping
neutrality leaves an individual semi-decisive over a proportion of pairs that
approaches one as the number of states grows.

The pattern across the whole literature, which is the point of the chapter: each
weakening of collective rationality converts the impossibility into a
concentration of power rather than removing it, and the concentration gets
harder to see without getting much smaller.

# Exercises

1. In Step 2, why does the proof need $x$ to be unplaced for
   $G_2 \setminus G_1$? Show what goes wrong if you give them $x \succ y \succ z$
   instead.

2. Show that under the Pareto-extension rule, $II$ also fails. Does $PI$?

3. The oligarchy $G^*$ is decisive *as a group*. Show that a proper subset of
   $G^*$ need not be semi-decisive, so "every member has a veto" does not
   collapse into "every member is decisive".

4. Suppose we add Non-dictatorship to the quasi-transitive framework. What does
   the theorem then tell us, and why is this not an impossibility result?

5. Compare the two escapes we have now seen. Single-peakedness restricts the
   domain and majority rule then works. Quasi-transitivity weakens the output
   and we get an oligarchy. Which is the better bargain, and on what grounds?
